title: Stormlight
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 9 of 10
content:
The storm came from two directions.

One was the ordinary sea, grey and furious beyond Tideglass Cove. The other blew through an unfinished Threadway, carrying rain that tasted of iron and sending sparks down the old lantern chain.

By the time the first bell rang, three houses near the shore had flooded.

Maui ran toward the water with his hook raised. I ran toward the square with the plans we'd drawn for the cove's drains.

We met halfway, both breathless, both angry.

“I can hold the waves,” he said, planting his hook against the wind. “I've made the ocean blink first. I can do it again.”

“For how long?”

“As long as I have to.”

“And then what?”

He looked at the houses, and I saw the calculation behind his bravado. He could lift stones and alter the current for a while, but the opening would keep pulling more water through.

“I need help,” he said.

It was not loud. The storm nearly swallowed it.

“I have a plan,” I answered.

The plan stopped being a plan as soon as people began asking real questions.

At the bakery door, Mara stood with a tray of bread she hadn't been able to move before the first floodwater reached the lower street. Pip was guiding residents toward the higher path, but the lantern on the corner had gone out. Neri had a list of safe rooms and no way to know which households were still below the tide markers.

"Can we open the hall?" I asked.

"We can," Neri said. "But only if someone checks the doors and keeps the exits clear. People need to know they can leave when they choose."

"I'll take the western stair," Pip offered.

"With another person," Neri said. "The boards might be wet."

Maui listened while someone from the cove described water lifting against their kitchen step. He held his hook with both hands.

"I could pull the whole house up," he said.

"Not with people inside," Fen answered sharply. They had arrived soaked, carrying their tide notes in a waxed pouch. "You'll split the foundation. Tell me where the current comes from."

I spread the map over a sheltered crate. The sketch from our earlier work showed the lower traveler arch and the shallow channel that led toward the harbor. It didn't show the new flow pushing through the unfinished Threadway.

"We need the waterline at the eastern post," I said.

Fen supplied it.

"And the tide direction?"

"Against the wind. That means the opening is feeding it."

I marked the arrows. A boulder would divert the flow toward the gardens. The loose brass ring was vibrating out of alignment again, but the older brace had been salvaged for another repair and the replacement had never been finished.

I felt a sharp flash of anger. We had known the part needed work.

Maui saw my face.

"Not now," he said softly.

"Not now," I agreed.

A family came up the square steps carrying two wet blankets and a sleepy child. Neri asked whether they wanted the hall or the upper route toward a Threadway. They chose the hall. Nobody demanded they explain where they would go afterward.

Mara set the tray down and handed out bread. "One piece each to start. I'll bring more after I check the ovens."

It wasn't an inspiring speech. It was exactly what we needed.

I sent Pip and another volunteer to the lantern corner with a safe replacement; Fen took the tideboard team. Only then did Maui and I return to the arch. It was frightening to realize the people we'd left behind were making decisions without us.

It was also the reason the plan could work.

At the breach, the air tasted metallic. Maui braced the fallen beam while I tested the ring's movement. The first attempt drove the current harder through the wrong side. We stopped, retreated to dry footing, and drew the new measurements in the mud on a board.

When the beam slipped, Maui planted his feet and let out a roar that carried over the storm.

"All right, water! You've had your fun. Now it's my turn!"

"Don't argue with an ocean," I shouted back.

"I've been arguing with the ocean longer than you've been alive!"

Mini Maui clung to the tattooed edge of his shoulder, drawing an exaggerated picture of the snapped support. He noticed, swore, and shifted his grip before the beam could twist in his hands. The boast had not saved the joint. His strength had bought us the seconds to get out of its way.

Fen called for the next reading. Maui threw them a look that plainly said he would rather punch the storm. He counted the beats between surges instead.

"Go on," he called to me. "Tell the hero where to hold the impossible thing."

"The left side. Only until Fen says stop."

"Terrible instructions. Very specific. Love it."

He braced the left side and kept watching Fen's raised hand. Even at his loudest, he hadn't forgotten whose call would keep us alive.

"Tell me the next step," he said.

"I don't know yet."

"Then we'll find it."

For once he didn't pretend certainty was an extra kind of strength. I showed him where the line needed to hold the ring while I seated the catch. He checked whether I could release my hand safely before we began.

We called Fen over to verify the current would not move into the houses when it changed. They studied the marks and gave us a short window between surges.

Only then did we go back into the rain.

We worked side by side. Neri organized neighbors into teams to move people to higher ground. Maui shifted the largest fallen timbers out of the paths without leaving me alone at the breach. I climbed the stable side of the old bridge and called measurements back to him. Together we set the brass ring into its proper groove and secured it with a brace made from the very dock he had rebuilt for us.

The Threadway shuddered. The wind reversed. Water poured back toward the sea.

For one terrifying moment the brace began to bend.

Maui braced it with his hook. I locked the final catch.

The storm on the other side went silent.

We stood in the sudden ordinary rain, shaking.

“Did we do it?” I asked.

Maui looked down at the ring, then at me.

“We did.”

Neri asked the people at the shelter not to rush back down the flooded road.

"A closed gate can be opened after a check," they said. "A damaged step can fail under somebody who thinks the danger has passed."

Mara sent bread and hot water across the square. One family wanted to stay with neighbors rather than enter the hall. Neri explained which route had been checked and let them choose.

Fen counted the tide markers again. Pip hung a temporary warning where the lamps had gone out. Nobody assumed a lantern was safe just because its wick could still light.

Maui looked at the shattered dock brace we'd used at the arch.

"I made that," he said.

"And you gave it up when we needed it," I answered.

He touched the splintered wood.

"Guess we'll build another."

"We'll ask what people need first."

He smiled despite his exhaustion.

"You're going to keep reminding me."

"Yes."

"Good."

People emerged from the workshop shelter, counting one another and checking for injuries. There was damage everywhere: mud in the gardens, broken steps, a smashed boat. Nothing had been magically made whole by saving the village.

I helped Neri make a list of repairs. Maui carried the heavy pieces where they were needed. When someone began calling him the greatest hero in the valley, he shook his head.

“Don't forget the people who built the plan.”

He pointed to me, then to the others who had helped.

I almost protested out of habit.

Instead I said, “And don't forget who moved the beams.”

He grinned, relieved.

That evening, exhausted, we sat on the dry steps of the bakery. I rested my head against his shoulder and watched the lanterns come on one by one.

“I remembered something in the storm,” I said.

He waited.

“I used to think the only reason anyone needed me was that I could solve things.”

“That's not true.”

“I know.” I swallowed. “I know it now.”

He slipped an arm around me only after I leaned closer.

The storm had left work for tomorrow. We did not have to do all of it tonight.

And the people who would help us were already setting chairs around the square.
